newsitem.title: USA: Healthy breast tissue may hold cancer clues.
newsitem.headline: Healthy breast tissue may hold cancer clues.

text.p: Apparently healthy breast tissue near a tumour can contain subtle genetic abnormalities that may give insight into how to treat specific tumours, a cancer researcher said Thursday.

The finding may also shed new light on how cancers form, said Helene Smith, a molecular biologist at California Pacific Medical Centre and University of California at San Francisco. Her research appears Friday in the journal Science.
In about one out of three of the tumours studied, her team found abnormalities called loss of heterozygosity, when healthy copies of tumour suppressor genes are lost.
Smith stressed that this has no immediate implications for treatment, and that it should not re-open debate about whether to perform mastectomies or the less extreme lumpectomy surgery.
"This exists. It's a phenomenon that we need to be thinking about," she told Reuters. "It's a little too soon to see how it plays out clinically."

About 10 percent of women who have lumpectomy and radiation have a local recurrence, a subsequent tumour in the breast. Smith wants to learn whether this genetic trait can identify those 10 percent at risk.
"Can we identify those women and take out more of the lump?" she said.

And if doctors can pinpoint which parts of a patient's breast is prone to tumour formation and which tissue is truly healthy, "we may be able to spare some radiation," she said, by targeting it only at the vulnerable sections.

Smith said researchers are also intrigued as to why this genetic abnormality occurs in one portion of the body and not in all cells. One theory, as yet unproven, is that the genetic change occurred before puberty in stem cells that would later turn into breast tissue.
